summary: A roughly 21-minute one-to-one in which Michael Brideau screen-shares and reviews a recorded call Richard Claessen ran with a prospect named Jess, stopping repeatedly to rework the first two minutes. Michael's diagnosis is that the call was lost in the opening minute because Richard opened with an uncalibrated comment about the prospect being 'laid out' on his phone, built no rapport, and then answered defensively for the rest of the call. He models his own opening verbatim — rapport, a 45-minute time frame, pen and paper, then 'what could we potentially help you with' — and models a mid-call reset for a disengaged prospect. The last third leaves the call itself and becomes personal: Michael attributes Richard's resistance to pride and self-guilt, recommends the book Letting Go and a journalling exercise, and asks unprompted about Richard's dating life and standards.
notable: MANAGER TAKES A PERFORMANCE REVIEW INTO PERSONAL PSYCHOLOGICAL TERRITORY — after the call review concludes, Michael asks 'is there a big, do you, do you find like, how's your, how's your dating life been? What's the patterns in your dating life right now? Are you dating anybody?' and Richard answers about his standards and his friends' observations. Michael also diagnoses 'there is a little bit of pride that you're not aware of', 'I can tell you put a lot of self guilt on yourself, dude', and 'there's a little bit of fear that you have to sit and process through', prescribing the book Letting Go and 'that journaling exercise'. This is a manager doing unsolicited quasi-therapeutic work on a direct report inside a recorded work call.

THE REVIEWED PROSPECT DISCLOSED A REPEATING INJURY CYCLE AND THE COACHING TREATED IT PURELY AS A RAPPORT PROBLEM — the prospect on the recording says 'I get injured every time I work out', 'I do weight training, and I go to get in shape, and I go for about a month or two, and I'll end up injuring myself, and then I need to sit out', and 'I'm done with having this cycle'. Michael's coaching is entirely about energy, rapport and framing; the correct handling he models is to position the programme as what breaks the cycle. Medical screening, contraindication and clinician clearance are never mentioned by either man.

The prescribed opening frame Michael models live is three-part, not the four-part frame the playbook specifies: 'I just want to kind of get a really good sense of like where we're at, what our goals are, what we're trying to accomplish' and elsewhere 'where you're at, where you want to get to, what's getting in the way'. 'What you need' is absent from both renditions.

Michael instructs that a badly-opened call should be reset rather than abandoned, and models the reset verbatim: 'bro, give me a second. Okay, dude, I think we need to start over because I think we're just not on the same foot with this conversation'. He also uses a founder-credibility line in that reset — 'Trevor's worked with like a thousand plus people and had amazing results and amazing transformations'.

Richard's stated standing policy is to disqualify prospects on posture and setting: 'if they're laid out like this with their phone and I'm like, mate, you book in this meeting, you want to get help, I'm here to help you, but then also actually show up professionally' and 'usually I wouldn't even want to go at further than this. I would just be like, nevermind.' Michael pushes back hard, calling it prideful. A rep-level disqualification habit on non-substantive grounds is a leakage risk worth quantifying.

Richard proposes recycling the burned lead to another rep — 'You can give him a call and say, oh, Rich, you're a new person' — and Michael refuses on capacity rather than principle: 'That's not the answer here, dude. The answer is you need to fix this. And I don't, I don't have time to call him.'
No recording disclosure appears in the transcript; the call opens mid-conversation about nicotine pouches.
